speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in respect to the Department of Defence Production I would like to refer briefly to both the department's traditional responsibility in the field of defence procurement and the additional undertakings that are being assumed in the purchasing and supply field for the civil departments of the government. I propose to deal initially with the Department of Defence Production, and when consideration of that is completed to tackle separately, and I hope in order, the emergency measures organization and, if we have time following that, the National Research Council.
The Department of Defence Production is responsible for the procurement of goods and services for the Department of National Defence, and also for ensuring that the necessary production capability is available to support our defence production program and related activities.
In addition, as I mentioned last year in my statement on the departmental estimates, the department is continuing to implement the recommendations of the royal commission on government organization which relate to departmental purchasing and supply responsibilities. In this connection as I indicated last year, the government, has approved the establishment within the department of a central purchasing agency to serve all departments and agencies of the federal government other than the commercially oriented crown corporations. The government has also approved the establishment of the basis for an integrated supply service.
Although it would not be appropriate to review all the procurement programs of the department at this time, I would like to draw the committee's attention to several areas of activity.
June 13, 1967

Supply-Defence Production
In shipbuilding a study of government procurement policies resulted in the adoption by the government of the principle that national competition should be sought whenever the nature and operational circumstances of the requirement so permitted. Procedures have now been introduced to let shipbuilding work competitively. Results of this policy have been successful.
A contract has been awarded to the Saint John Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Company Limited for the construction of two operational support ships for the Royal Canadian Navy. This is the largest shipbuilding contract ever placed in Canada, and these two ships will increase the fleet's anti-submarine warfare potential by keeping our destroyers at sea for a longer period than is now possible.
The modernization and refit of seven destroyer escorts of the St. Laurent class was completed in the fall of 1966. Work on the modernization of the first of seven vessels of the Restigouche class is being undertaken by H.M.C. Dockyard, Halifax. The six following vessels will be modernized by commercial shipyards selected through competitive tenders. The work on the first of these ships is scheduled to commence in January, 1968.
Production contracts for new and advanced sonar systems for these ships are in progress. New data processing methods for anti-submarine warfare are being developed which will result in a significant improvement in the ships' capabilities, and new communications systems are to be installed using a unique method of switching to permit common use of antennae, thus reducing deck clutter. Studies are under way to establish a method of electronically monitoring all the ships' systems in order to improve maintenance procedures.
The first of the three Oberon class submarines being procured from the British ministry of defence, the Ojibwa, was delivered in September, 1965 and the second submarine, the Onondaga, which was lauched the same month is scheduled for delivery in mid-1967. The Okanagan is scheduled for delivery in mid-1968.
Four vessels are being constructed for the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in support of their hydrographic, oceanographic and linographic research programs in international, Canadian coastal and great lakes waters. Under this program contracts were awarded late in 1965 for two tidal and current survey vessels, with completion scheduled for August and October, 1967. Contracts for two other research vessels were awarded

in 1966 with completion scheduled for August, 1967 and May, 1968.
A contract for a naval research establishment vessel required to provide an oceangoing research facility for acoustic, antisubmarine warfare, hydrographic and oceanographic research was awarded in November, 1966, as a result of competitive tenders. Completion of the vessel is scheduled for early 1969.
In the field of communications, consultants are completing a comprehensive study of the design of a modern communication system for the Department of National Defence. In addition a wide range of equipments is being purchased to provide communications for the operational elements of our forces.
In the aircraft field, in addition to the production of the 115 CF-5 aircraft for the Canadian armed forces, significant programs include the de Havilland Buffalo aircraft. Progress on our own military order for 15 of these aircraft is satisfactory, and 12 aircraft have been sold commercially in the export market. Current and prospective sales of the de Havilland twin engine Otter aircraft, which features the Canadian designed and manufactured PT6 turboprop engine, justify our initial confidence in and financial support of these two programs.

The first of seven Falcon Dassault transport aircraft was accepted in Paris several weeks ago. The Canadian industry must prepare plans for the electronic systems that it will have to install; it will also furnish the seven aircraft.
Ten Bell tactical transport helicopters are also being purchased for the Canadian armed forces.

Export sales of the Canadian designed and produced Black Brant research rockets are being made by Bristol Canada whose facilities are able to offer quick delivery to potential customers.
Modernization programs, including the fitment of new avionic equipment, are being carried out on such aricraft as the CS2F Tracker, Argus and Neptune anti-submarine warfare aeroplanes and CHSS-2 Sea King helicopters. My departmental officers are also collaborating with the aerospace industry and other nations in a number of interesting development projects with good market potential. For example, the CL84 vertical and short
June 13, 1967	COMMONS
take off and landing dynavert is now being evaluated by the United States.
While we may tend to emphasize the development and production of new aircraft, there are also contracts placed, totalling some $70 million annually, for the repair of aerospace equipment, with 40 to 50 contractors from coast to coast in Canada.
The Department of Defence Production is also continuing to procure various types of conventional weapons and ammunition to meet the training requirements of the Canadian defence forces. To the extent feasible these requirements are produced in Canada.
The recent development of the anti-submarine projectile which has now been introduced into the Canadian navy has resulted in substantial sales of this item to Britain and to the Netherlands. Canadian development of the Dance lightweight launcher is on schedule. This development is being supported under the Canada-United States defence development and production sharing program. Already an initial production order has been received as a result of development work.
Negotiations have also been completed for the procurement of 800 military type jeeps to replace similar vehicles bought during the Korean conflict. Delivery was obtained on the majority of the 150 aircraft refuelling trucks previously ordered for support of the air service at home and abroad. Action is now under way to purchase Lynx command and reconnaissance vehicles, self propelled 155 mm. Jiowitzers, and Ram trucks to replace the present M37 cargo trucks.

The complexity of military equipment required to meet the most modest and limited defensive roles is continously increasing. This expansion in technical sophistication arises from the necessity to achieve greater flexibility of application and, by increased automation, to raise the efficiency of employment of military manpower. These factors contribute substantially to the steady rise in the cost of developing and producing modern defence equipment, which has been evident in the past few years and which is expected to continue in the future.
In common with our allies we seek to achieve maximum cost effectiveness in the application of our necessary defence budgets. This means that every defence procurement contemplated must be considered not only in the sense of military necessity but also in regard to many interrelated economic factors. We must strive to obtain the best equipment for the lowest cost while at the same time considering the importance of the procurement to the maintenance of an essential minimum Canadian industrial defence base and the extent to which it may contribute to our over-all national economic growth.
Our allies are generally faced with the same considerations and it is becoming increasingly apparent that in many cases our mutual interests are best served by co-operative development and production. By such means the cost reduction advantages attendant on larger scale production can be realized. At the same time the development investment and risk can be shared and the participating nations afforded the opportunity to specialize in fields of technology appropriate to their resources and interests. The number of such co-operative projects is steadily increasing, involving not only the smaller nations but also the larger powers who in spite of their extensive industrial resources are finding it progressively more uneconomical to justify independent development and production. The difficulties inherent in putting together multi-national defence equipment programs are very great, but expertise is being developed in Canada which is being put to good use.
It would not be practical to review all such projects in which Canada is involved at present or likely to be in the future. I would, however, like to refer to two typical projects now in being. First in the aricraft field, where production of 115 CF-5 aircraft for the Canadian armed forces is proceeding on
June 13, 1967

Supply-Defence Production schedule, the government of the Netherlands has now confirmed its desire to participate in the Canadian production of the CF-5 tactical ground support fighter. The Netherlands air force is in the process of placing orders for 105 aircraft and associated spares, which will have the effect of almost doubling the production requirement over the next four years. This arrangement offers potential savings to both governments in production costs and the lifetime maintenance expenses for the aircraft. Expanded navigation and other facilities are being added by the Netherlands thus further increasing the flexibility and effectiveness of this aircraft in certain roles. Both the Canadian and Netherlands aerospace industries will be co-operating in the manufacture of the many components and subassemblies required, and this association offers the opportunity to develop advantageous longer term industrial trading relations.
Second, in the area of battlefield surveillance systems Canada, Britain and Germany have co-operated in the development in Canada of the CL-89 reconnaissance drone. The three countries shared the cost of this successful development on an equal basis and are currently planning production to start later this year to meet their joint requirements. By sharing the cost and the risk the three countries will thus be able to acquire essential advanced defensive equipment for a minimum investment.
The department will continue to explore and develop all such opportunities for cooperation wherever it appears in the best interests of Canada and of our allies.
As a step toward the implementation of the recommendations of the royal commission on government organization, a thorough evaluation of defence acquisition methods and techniques indicated early in 1966 the possibility of a significant improvement in departmental management of major defence procurement projects. Accordingly it was decided to establish a program of single office project management within which a single officer would be assigned appropriate authority and responsibility for managing all aspects of the implementation phase of selected procurement projects. The primary responsibility of these project managers will be to maintain the time, cost and performance objectives established by the funding authorities.

Supply-Defence Production

The result of having both a consolidated service and skilful people engaged in operating it will, I hope, be that the occasions on which the government finds itself with overstocking or being left with obsolete or obsolescent stocks on its hands will decline quite materially. Virtually all the electronic controls, and they are becoming more and more widespread now, have both a civilian and a military application. In many cases, if not the whole system at least significant components are the same for both civil and military use. This means that defence production, which classically perhaps could be limited to a few arsenals producing specialized military equipment such as guns, tanks, certain electronic equipment and the like, was unique to the military, but it is no longer unique. Indeed, to furnish the equipment for a modern military force requires the output of virtually all our manufacturing concerns-I emphasize, all of them, particularly the more sophisticated- and requires the output of some manufacturing concerns which we do not have in Canada and which, because of the small domestic volume of Canadian demand, it would not make economic sense for us to have in Canada.
So the decision was taken to endeavour, where military weapons systems were concerned, to specialize in Canada in the production of either elements of systems or systems themselves in which we could have and could expect to have a proficiency and an efficiency to manufacture economically, not only for ourselves but also for export. In this way it was considered that we would have a large enough unit of the market, which means a large enough unit of production, that the process of the particular manufacturer would be economic in current industrial terms. If we are to specialize our production for a limited number of items for our own forces, we must import the balance of our needs.

If this were the prospect, if we could at least hope to compete in the continental market as distinct from the limited Canadian market, I think our yards on the west coast would have a genuine opportunity of not only surviving but looking forward to a period of expansion.

Private Bills

The question which immediately comes to my mind is that if this company had a specific plan to construct a 12-inch main line from a point near Calgary in the province of Alberta through various mountain ranges to the coast at or near the port of Vancouver, this would be a major project and our approach to it would be quite different. If the bill then received second reading in the house and went before a committee for study, the committee would have something into which it could put its teeth. In such a case the committee could endeavour to make a rational examination of the project on the basis of its feasibility, the existing state of technical knowledge of the best method of transferring sulphur in this form, and the impact which the proposed pipe line system, whereby sulphur would be transferred from the gas fields of Alberta to a seaport outlet, would have on the existing railway lines and their potential capacity to transport the product in modern bunker cars.
I think all of us recognize the massive capital investment which has been made in our existing railway system. Certainly those of us from British Columbia are well aware of the high cost of engineering and construction of railway lines through that part of Canada, and all of us recognize it is quite an important consideration to the economic health of this country that the railways operate in a manner that is economically healthy. These are some of the factors which I think a committee of the house could intelligently weigh if the company had come before us with a definite proposal to construct a specific line.
However, this is not what we have in the bill. Although we can certainly accept without question the statement made by the sponsor of the bill that the company intends to undertake the project which he outlined in some detail, there is no such assurance contained in the bill. All we have here are broad, general provisions which will give this company the right to discard the proposal completely and to decide, for instance, that it will build a pipe line from Calgary to Hudson Bay and ship the sulphur to Hudson Bay for transmission through the port of Churchill.
We have listened to many discussions in the house concerning the virtue of building up the volume of shipping through the port of Churchill and the Hudson Bay route. Many of us, even though we may not come from that part of the country, recognize that this would be a very desirable development. But I submit

it is not desirable for parliament to give a blank cheque to a company such as this one.
Members such as the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra and the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, who represent the main coastal seaport of Vancouver, should perhaps demonstrate a more direct concern by investigating whether or not the company's proposal will benefit the development of the port of Vancouver. What is proposed in this bill will certainly not achieve this. I have been present at committee meetings when the publicly owned railway company has had to come before parliament with a specific project before being allowed to extend their railway lines to any extent. The vice president of Canadian National Railways in charge of engineering and development has had to place before the committee full details concerning the economics of the specific section of railway line to be built. This is not the approach of this company. We are presented with vague, all-embracing clauses in the bill on the basis of which we have to make a decision. We can set up these companies by the dozen if we choose. Indeed, parliament has done so over a period of years. Then, as was said the other day in connection with another bill, we rely upon the National Energy Board, with its rather vague terms of reference, to make other necessary decisions.
I am not certain whether the pipe line proposed under the bill would be under the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board or of the new Canadian Transportation Commission. However, I feel that transportation facilities should be regarded as a public utility and that a much more desirable approach would be to develop at least the main arteries of our national transportation system as a public utility under public ownership and control. But even apart from that consideration I feel it is not a good policy, from any point of view that may be held in this parliament, to give blanket approval to the incorporation of companies which would empower them to do what is sought under the bill now before us. I think we should say to the sponsors of this bill: If the Shell Oil Company and the related interests associated with this bill have a specific need to move sulphur from point A to point B, and if you can demonstrate to parliament that this can be an efficient and economic operation, one that will not operate to the detriment of existing transportation facilities, then parliament might be prepared to consider your proposal on its merits.

However, the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra-

The bill
before us, Mr. Speaker, is something in the nature of an iceberg in that one-tenth of it is on the surface and is obvious and nine tenths is unknown or is the subject of speculation. There are two aspects of the bill with which I should like to deal. The first concerns the venture into the bill of transportation by Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company and the change that this may bring about in the transportation industry as well as the economic effects that may flow therefrom. Then
Private Bills
there is the matter of the ownership of the company itself. As we all know, the Pear-son-Gordon duet on foreign ownership has been mentioned far and wide across the country. Reference has been made to foreign ownership on television by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) in his capacity as an author, a royal commissioner and a cabinet minister. We have dealt with this aspect in the house on previous bills. It may sound a bit like repetition but I think it is such an important aspect in our consideration of this company and its ownership that it bears repetition.
The philosophy enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to a nation-wide television audience supported entirely the position taken by the President of the Privy Council over the years, and it applies directly to the bill before us. This philosophy, I understand, advocates the repatriation of the ownership of our industry. It may be it is not possible to bring about repatriation overnight because the consequences which might flow from such action could be rather terrible if we ran into the threatened retaliation which our so-called friends to the south are not adverse to using whenever it suits their purpose. I believe the government has recognized the necessity of phasing the return of ownership of Canadian industry to Canadian hands. I believe an indication of that recognition can be seen in the Mercantile Bank situation in that Mercantile was given a period of time to comply with the law. Just a few days ago the United Investment Life Insurance Company had read into Hansard by the sponsor of its bill a commitment that it would phase out foreign ownership of the company it was seeking to have incorporated within a period of ten years. Perhaps the thought that should be uppermost in our minds at the moment is how we can get Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company into the hands of Canadians.
It seems much more difficult to do here than it has been in the case of companies which are controlled in the United States. Whether or not our difficulties are greater or less when companies are owned in other countries is more than I can say at the moment. As a preface to my remarks I should like to read from Hansard for June 1, page 852, where the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) was dealing with the ownership of this company. He is reported as having said:
With regard to Shell Canada Limited, which will be the principal shareholder of the new company, 17.5 per cent of the voting power is in the hands of

the public, and these shares are traded on the stock exchanges in Canada. The remaining 82.5 per cent is held by another Canadian company called Shell Investments Limited, the head office of which is also in Toronto.
Looking at the matter from that point, it appears as if Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company is going to be a Canadian owned company because 82.5 per cent of the shares are owned by a Canadian company and 17.5 per cent of the shares are in the hands of the general public. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra went on to say:
Shell Investments is in turn wholly owned by a Netherlands company situated at the Hague and, finally, the ownership of the company is divided as to 60 per cent in the hands of the Royal Dutch Petroleum Company at the Hague, and as to 40 per cent in the hands of the Shell Transport and Trading Company in London, England.

I have not worked out the intricacies of this to see who owns what, but I think it is fairly clear that Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company is owned or will be owned by the Royal Dutch Petroleum Company and Shell Transport and Trading Company, one company at The Hague in the Netherlands and the other in London, England. Therefore I think this is a situation we should seek to alter.
If I recall correctly, Mr. Speaker, the oil industry in Canada in one form or another is owned 100 per cent by foreign companies. There was one Canadian company, called if I am not mistaken Canadian Oils, which held out but finally went under a few years ago, giving over our entire oil industry in Canada to the hands of foreign companies controlled by people who are not Canadian citizens, who do not even live in this country and who give political allegiances, if these transcend profit ones, to other nations. There are in any event companies who look at their Canadian interests after they have concerned themselves with their major investments in other parts of the world.
I should like to see a declaration made by someone within this lineage of corporate ownership related by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, and made before the standing committee, that it is the intention of the company to divest itself over a reasonable period of time of its foreign ownership aspects, so that this company would become in fact a Canadian owned company, and thus at least emotionally identified with Canadian interests in the first instance.
Presumably the whole objective of the company, at least as I read the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, is to operate

at some time in the future a solids pipe line within Canada. This does not exempt them from the prospect of exporting by solids pipe line, because other commodities are exported by pipe line; but I think it would be far better if this company were a Canadian company and recognized that the declaration of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) carries some weight. I also think this parliament gave some expression to that declaration.
Perhaps this is a matter that could be dealt with in greater detail at the committee stage. I simply put the suggestion on the record now. At the appropriate time-perhaps at the committee stage so as to give the company fair warning in advance-I for one, and I know there are other members of the house of this view, should like to see the company come forward and declare that within a certain period of time, which I submit should not be an unreasonable one such as 50 years-ten years seems to be the period that has arbitrarily been decided on-the company will divest itself of its foreign ownership aspect and thus permit it truly to become a Canadian-owned company.
During the course of the last session, though it may have been during a private discussion on this bill, I gained the impression that the bill was introduced with the object of enabling the company to conduct research into the transmission of solids by pipe line. The sponsor of the bill relied on the fact that research is one of the activities of the company because he talked of the prospect of transmitting sulphur. As reported at page 852 of Hansard he said:
As sulphur has not so far been transported in solid form by pipe line on a commercial scale, research still has to be done before the company can be certain that this 750 mile pipe line from Alberta to the west coast is feasible. Since to a large extent the exact location of the route will be dependant on the outcome of the research and development program which is presently taking place and which will continue after incorporation of this company, no specific route can be designated, at this time. The company's confidence, however, can be measured by the large sums of money it has already spent and will spend in the next two years, if this bill is passed, in developing this research to maturity.
At the commencement of the remarks of the sponsor of the bill, after he had got through marrying the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford), in his first sentence related to the bill he said:
This bill deals with a company that wishes to operate a commercial solids pipe line.
Then as reported at page 852 he went on to deal with the cost aspect and the $50 million
June 13, 19S7

that it is estimated sulphur transmission alone will cost, the manner in which this would be financed, and so on.
If this is to be a research venture, Mr. Speaker, then I do not see the necessity for incorporating the company. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out in some detail, there are already a couple of solids pipe line research groups in existence, groups which have received public aid and in which there is a great deal of interest by Canadian National, Canadian Pacific and certain oil companies.
And well there might be interest by the Canadian National Railways in this aspect, Mr. Speaker, which gives me more concern than this particular company becoming a research operation. Because if we are now to embark, as I think we are, upon a project to replace the current transportation system with something of this kind, then we are likely to throw completely out of kilter the economy of a large part of this nation. For instance, the building of a line in my own constituency for the transmission of solids involving, for argument's sake, wood chips for a pulp mill may in itself be an economic move, but would cut into the financial and economic position of the Canadian National Railways Company and would undoubtedly injure and curtail its activities.
At the moment, Mr. Speaker, we are moving a tremendous amount of grain by railway. If research proves that it is feasible to move grain by pipe line, then this could practically destroy the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway as far as freight carriage of that commodity is concerned. Once we do this and impinge upon their income prospects by removing from them some of the products they now carry, we cut into the prospects of either one of these companies operating on any sort of economic basis.
I could mention other commodities. For example the sponsor of the bill mentioned coal having been moved in slurry form. Potash comes to mind as a commodity for potential movement by pipe line. Many more commodities and materials might be added to this list of potential materials for movement by pipe lines, and I would not like to see us embark upon a program of giving a carte blanche right to a foreign company to build and operate a solids pipe line anywhere in Canada for the movement of materials in Canada or for export. This would cause a great deal of disruption to our public transportation systems and to our economy.

[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
I am not opposed to change. In fact, I welcome change as well as anybody, but I like to see that change or alteration in our economic structure come about in such a way that dislocation is orderly, so that the working force which depends to such a great extent upon our current transportation method is not found out of existence and in the unemployment lines, simply to meet the convenience of Royal Dutch Petroleum or the Shell Investment Company, or for that matter whoever is behind this company. I do not want to see change or alteration come about in such a way as to pull the economic rug out from under any other communities in this country which depend to a great extent on our current transportation systems for their livelihood.
The research aspect of this whole proposal should be of concern to the public of Canada and this parliament. After all, this is the public's business with which we are dealing, rather than the affair of a few people named in clause 1 of the bill, or those who may become the shareholders or directors in the future. We have gone far beyond the stage when we could consider a bill such as this and its impact on our economy as a private matter to be dealt with only to meet the convenience of its promoters. This bill, perhaps more so than any other legislation placed before this parliament in some time, has an aura of public importance about it. It should perhaps be treated by parliament as a public bill, because its importance demands that parliament consider not only the foreign aspect of it but the public welfare, in light of the complete disruption that may result to many communities, workers and areas of our economy. If this is a gamble, and I am not so sure that it is, it should be considered seriously in that light. I suggest it is not as much of a gamble as one might think. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) in his opening remarks pointed out that the confidence of this company could be measured by the amount it has spent and will spend in the next few years. I see that you are rising, Mr. Speaker, and I assume that my time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, when this bill came before us on the last occasion we had an opportunity of discussing some of our objections with officials of the company. It was interesting to note

June 13, 1967
Private Bills
that they were in agreement in respect of one contention I had, namely that this was an exceptionally important bill which would have as great an effect on the transportation facilities in our country as a third transcontinental railroad. Anyone who considers the prospect of a third railroad across Canada must realize immediately how the construction of this line would affect the transportation facilities existing in this nation.
It has been agreed by a great many individuals with knowledge in this field that this should not only be of interest to members of the opposition but also to members of the government. When this bill goes to the committee there should be some indication on the part of government members and other opposition members that they realize the implications involved in the creation of a totally new company to move solids by pipe line. The other day when we were talking about rainmaking equipment, considerable interest was expressed about the technical feasibility. I am sure there are many members who have not really thought about this particular bill and are not aware of the fact that it is within the technical knowledge of many companies to move many types of commodities by pipe line. Many basic commodities in capsule forms can be moved through pipe lines. This would eliminate the need for large commodity handling facilities.
When discussing this proposal with officials of the company, it was pointed out that they were well aware that the sulphur they intended to move would have to be put into slurry form, and that after it was transported to its destination the sulphur would have to be taken out of the slurry vehicle. It was not known whether the same quantity of sulphur put in could be taken out at the destination point. The suggestion was made that certain types of oil could be used as the vehicle, because sulphur is found originally in that oil. They felt that perhaps the proportion of the sulphur in the slurry could be increased to 90 per cent, but there still would be some difficulty in removing that sulphur from the slurry and some uncertainty as to the type of facility required.
If I lived in the area of the transmission destination, for example in the Richmond area of Vancouver, I would be very skeptical about having that type of facility located there in order to take this sulphur from the slurry, particularly if it involved a method similar to that used for removing the sulphur from the oil in the refinery. The disagreeable smell which often exists in Ottawa, when the

wind is blowing from Gatineau Pointe, I suggest is mild to what might be the smell at the terminal point of one of these solids pipe line. However, I suppose it is up to members who live in such an area to decide whether the location of the terminal there would be advantageous. Perhaps they are not interested in that aspect.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that it is technically easy to move these commodities by pipe line. I am sure that not only sulphur could be moved from sources in Saskatchewan, but also the potash that is produced there. This potash could be moved to markets on the west coast by putting it into slurry form, through the use of water or some other vehicle. In this manner it could be moved over the mountains to Vancouver at a rate cheaper than the railway companies are able to offer.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Every time I ride on the railway I am reminded of the lack of interest the railway companies show in my comfort and in the comfort of others travelling on the trains. I might therefore be expected to say that I have not much interest in railway affairs. However, if we look at the role the railways play in the movement of commodities we are bound to realize it is an important one and that there will probably always be commodities more suited to travel by rail than by pipe line.
Including human beings.

Yes. I am not sure I am prepared to travel through the mountains in a capsule propelled through a pipe line. It might come to that in the future but I am not sure I am prepared for it. Bad as they may be, trains are preferable to capsule travel.
The problem facing the government is not a technical one. In Britain the movement of coal by pipe line has proved feasible, and technical difficulties in the way of the movement of sulphur and oil are in sight of solutions. As the use of these methods develops however it is likely that many basic commodities in this country could be moved quickly and economically by pipe line.
This competition would obviously have an adverse effect upon the position of the railroads; they might even be threatened with extinction. But if there were no railroads, what would happen in the case of those many commodities which it would still be necessary to move by rail? Suppose a decision was made to keep the railways going, in any case.
June 13, 1967

Would not the cost to the shipper and to the
public be extremely high? With these things in mind, I believe the government must show some interest in pipe lines as a form of transportation. If the government would assure us that it was willing to carry out research to determine the end result of successful pipe line operations of the kind which are contemplated in the bill before us, then I think we would be prepared to send this measure to a committee where further discussion could take place.
The committee to which this bill would normally be sent is, in my submission, not competent to make a decision on the questions of principle I have raised. This is because it lacks the necessary information, the necessary research data. Then again, I believe many of its members would not be interested in reaching a decision in connection with the broader policy matters I have outlined.
I am aware that the transportation commissioners will have some control over this situation as a result of a section in the new act which brings solids pipe lines within their jurisdiction. But the examination of the relationship between pipe lines and the transportation system and other types of transportation in Canada cannot be undertaken by the committee, and will have to be undertaken by the government itself outside the committee. I am of the opinion that the government will have to reach a policy decision about the development of solids pipe lines. If the company wishes to do the necessary research into the feasibility of carrying certain commodities between specific points, this could be considered by the committee. But it seems to me that when we are confronted by an entirely new form of transportation the government itself should be interested in ascertaining what the end result will be before allowing a company to establish a monopoly in handling a particular commodity.
I do not think it would be difficult for the transport commissioners to arrive at equitable rates as between this form of transport and others under their jurisdiction. But this would not solve the broader problem to which I have referred. Many of the major products of the prairie provinces can now be moved by pipe line. Before too long it will probably be possible to move wheat by this method.
What would be the result? It might well be possible to transport grain more economically and at the same time to remove much of the dissatisfaction which has existed over the years in connection with the handling of this commodity at port terminals. Many of the

Supply-Defence Production bottlenecks which now occur in the railway yards of Vancouver could be removed. As I say, our main consideration should be the effect this would have on the operation of the railways. I agree with previous speakers that it is important there should be as much Canadian control over pipe line transportation as possible.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just spoken asked me what general progress there had been in the matter of increasing the economic usefulness of the shipyards on the west coast as a consequence of the new program in respect of government shipbuilding activities which was initiated about two years ago. The answer in general terms is that I think this is proving reasonably successful.
It will be remembered that representations were made at that time that, because the then current costs of shipbuilding on the west coast were higher than elsewhere in Canada,
[Mr. Harkness.i
the translation of government procurement from a system of allocation by a government commission to one of full and free national price competition would not allow an appropriate or reasonable period for the west coast shipyards to rearrange themselves on a rather more competitive basis with what were reported to be lower costs in east coast and St. Lawrence river shipyards.

As a consequence, it was agreed that in respect of national competitive contracts there would be an allocation of a specific total tonnage year by year over a five year period as a minimum assured volume of business for the west coast yards regardless of national price competition. Because of the assured business, it was hoped that it would be easier for the west coast shipyards to adjust to a policy of full national competition. Over the course of the past two years we have observed, in respect of government shipbuilding contracts on the west coast as well as on the east coast and the St. Lawrence yards, that the west coast yards, although they have not been the lowest bidders, on occasion have been the second or third lowest bidder. Mr. Chairman, I was wondering whether the minister would say something about the Emergency Measures Organization which is covered by this vote. There are a few remarks I should like to make on it. It seems to me that the Emergency Measures Organization is languishing; at least, I have seen and heard very little about it during the last year or two. It would appear that there is not very much energy or drive being put into the Emergency Measures Organization program. We used to have an annual meeting of dominion and provincial
June 13. 1967

Supply-Defence Production representatives with regard to emergency measures matters. I have not heard of any of these meetings being held for some time. In fact, if my memory is correct, only one has been held in the last four years.
I found these extremely useful meetings. They did a great deal to maintain interest and to ensure that the same sort of measures and programs were being put into effect throughout Canada. I do not know whether this part of the program has been terminated. I do not know when the last of these meetings was held and when the next one is to be held. In the circumstances we would like these questions answered.
Also, Mr. Chairman, there used to be at least one annual exercise a year more or less on a national basis, as well as a number on a regional basis. I have heard of no exercises along these lines having taken place. There may have been some regional exercises carried out, and I hope this has been the case. I know there have been some in Alberta, at least on a regional basis if not on a provincial basis. I do not know whether there have been any others. It so happens that Alberta, which is the province I come from, has been more active and energetic than any other province in regard to the activities of the Emergency Measures Organization. I do not think there have been any national exercises carried out.
It seems to me that if the Emergency Measures Organization is to be kept in a reasonable degree of efficiency, exercises are essential in order to maintain their expertise in these various matters and to test their operational efficiency. Thus they would be in a position to make improvements in the whole Emergency Measures Organization setup.
I also ask, what has happened as far as the warning system is concerned? This used to be carried on to a great extent by the army; nuclear detonation reporting centres were maintained by the army outside all the larger cities and other stations were maintained by provincial officials, and so forth. The army having withdrawn from this activity, I wonder what the state of efficiency is, as far as the warning system is concerned.
Equally important in this regard is the state of the communications set-up, which was also operated to a large extent by the army. Who is now operating the Emergency Measures Organization communications set-up, and is it geared to meet an emergency if one should occur? I know that in the last three or four years there has been a general feeling, not

only in Canada but in other parts of the world, that there has been an easing of tensions between eastern and western blocs of nations, and perhaps, naturally, there was less interest in the Emergency Measures Organization and its functions generally than was the case a few years ago. However, Mr. Chairman, as long as the threat of nuclear attack exists-and I think everyone will admit that threat does still exist-I think it is essential for the protection of the population of Canada that an efficient Emergency Measures Organization be kept in operation. I have been more and more concerned that this is not being done and that this organization generally has been allowed to die, or at least languish. The various programs that were being actively carried on seem to be no longer in operation at all, or they are not being pursued very actively.
Another program about which to my knowledge we have heard absolutely nothing, in the last two or three years is the shelter program. The last time I heard about this program was when I asked the minister a question about it in the house two or three years ago. At that time, as I recall, he said that a survey of all public buildings, federal and provincial, which had previously been initiated was still being maintained and he expected it to be completed fairly soon. The minister said this survey would give us information with regard to what types of shelter and what degree of shelter existed. I have heard nothing of this program for some considerable time. I wonder what the situation is in this regard. I ask the minister whether the survey has been completed; and if it has been completed, what use is being made of the information being collected? This program was quite extensive and cost the Canadian taxpayer a considerable amount of money. I hope that some use is being made of the information secured by the survey.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that I intended to make only a few brief remarks. I hope the minister will be able to tell us what the situation is and what it has been during the last two or three years with regard to the Emergency Measures Organization.

All equipment and supplies are packaged into operational units, and arrangements are being made for the responsible provincial organizations to take charge of these supplies.
The Canadian forces, in addition to their responsibilities for warning, continue to develop their capability to direct and conduct rescue operations, should this prove to be necessary.
The public education program of Canada E.M.O. has been oriented toward having readily available a wide range of information so that should a demand arise, it would be able to respond to that demand. I do not believe that it is necessary, or even desirable, in the present state of international tension to keep vivid in the minds of the public the importance of survival preparations.
These are a few of many activities which are directed to the first national objective.
The second national objective, which is directed toward the maintenance of government under nuclear war conditions, also shows continuing progress. In addition to a complex of protected facilities outside the Ottawa area, there are in existence in six provinces protected headquarters from which components of the provincial and federal governments would operate. The remaining four provinces, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan, have interim facilities available. During the next four or five years it is our intention to develop longer term facilities for those provinces, as well as continuing to improve the emergency facilities already provided in the other provinces.
Below the provincial level, Canada E.M.O. has been working closely with their provincial counterparts to provide protected facilities from which municipal governments would be able to operate. I am told by the provinces that there are approximately 130 of these headquarters in existence and operational.
This network of emergency government headquarters, from federal down to municipal levels, is tied together by a comprehensive communications system.

Much remains to be done in this general area, but as each year passes additional elements are added and improvements continue to take place.
In working toward our third national objective-the effective management of surviving resources-much of the work is carried out by the responsible federal department, co-ordinated as necessary by the Emergency Measures Organization. Emergency plans are in existence and are under constant review, to manage supplies of all kinds; to continue the productive capacity of our agricultural and fishing industries; and to operate the communications and transportation industries. Work is continuing in the areas of emergency manpower planning, control of accommodation and engineering, and construction resources.
Needless to say, although most of the work in these areas is under the direction of the federal government, the achievements to date would not have taken place had we not received the co-operation of the appropriate provincial departments, and of many hundreds of officials from business and industry.
Mr. Chairman, hon. members should note that seven or eight years ago very few of these measures or activities were in existence. Today they are. Many of them were started by the previous government. And this, I think, bears out the observation I made earlier, that is to say, that with relatively modest annual expenditures a great deal can be done to improve our nation's capability to survive.
At this point I would like to pay tribute to some 150,000 volunteers who, over the years, have contributed significantly to the organization at the local level. Additionally I would like to express the thanks of the government to many thousands of federal, provincial and municipal employees who have accepted the responsibility for emergency planning as a functional extension of their peacetime responsibilities. This is the key to effective civil emergency planning. This ensures that we do not duplicate our efforts and that we make the best use of our existing resources to build up an effective emergency preparedness program.
The true function of the Emergency Measures Organization, be it at the federal, provincial or municipal level, is to co-ordinate emergency planning and to assist existing departments of government in developing their existing capability to meet emergency situations. It has never been the intention of this government, nor of past governments, to have

the Emergency Measures Organization usurp or replace the functional responsibility of governments or their departments at the time of an emergency, be it in peacetime or during a war emergency.

As I say, I think this idea is very worth while. Since the minister seems to be sending these hospitals freely, and perhaps is not aware of it, I should like to make a pitch for a few of them, if I may. A few months ago in this house I suggested that it was time that some members of the medical profession took part actively and voluntarily in giving aid to foreign countries such as Viet Nam, and perhaps South America and the Caribbean the

Supply-Defence Production idea being based on the method now being used in the United States and presently carried on in Viet Nam by civilian doctors, who go there on a rotational basis spending 60 days in Viet Nam.
These doctors come from right across the United States and I believe that at the present time there are 34 surgeons and medical men operating in Viet Nam helping civilian casualties in that country. Their services are given purely voluntarily. Perhaps this fits in with the plea recently made by the director general of external aid before the external affairs committee the other day, when he said he would like to see some voluntary work instead of just money going into this type of external aid. It seems to me, however, we had better rotate them a little more, because according to Dr. Vennema there is a great shortage of medical supplies even in the Canadian facility in South Viet Nam. I should like the minister to give serious consideration to my proposal, which has already received a lot of favourable support among members of the medical profession who have expressed their willingness to operate such a venture. The Canadian Medical Association, though it feels that our medical resources are perhaps a bit thin to send too many supplies to Viet Nam, is looking with a great deal of interest at this proposal and has already met with members of the government concerning such a program in South America and the Caribbean. This type of hospital, which can be transported in one of our large aircraft or sent by ship, could easily be set up in any available area, and with this sort of Canadian ingenuity I think the staff of the organization certainly deserve credit for designing this type of hospital. speechtext:
Perhaps I may respond to the questions asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West and also say a word or two about the representation made by the hon. member for Saskatoon. The hon. member for Kootenay West asked what the Emergency Measures Organization does in respect to peacetime disasters. I tried to indicate in my general remarks that the role of the Emergency Measures Organization was one of coordinating and planning. Provided the various agencies of government have prepared adequate plans to cope with emergencies, there is really nothing for the E.M.O. to do. Its job is to ensure that adequate plans and preparations are made by the various levels of government and agencies responsible for carrying out particular functions. It is not the object of the E.M.O. to usurp or replace emergency operations of governments or agencies in Canada.
Let us consider as an example a flood threat in the Columbia river valley. There is a provincial government agency whose task it is to report on the threat of superabundant water as a result of surveys, meteorological reports and so forth. It is the job of a provincial government department to ensure that road communications in the Columbia river valley are in good condition at all times, including times of flood. It is the job of another department of the government to ensure that there is an adequate supply of water and electricity for municipalities in ordinary times and during disasters.
The role of the Emergency Measures Organization is to keep after these government departments to make sure they have adequate

plans and are making the necessary plans in the event that an anticipated disaster, in this case a flood, should occur. I am glad to say that the Emergency Measures Organization has met at the federal and provincial level and has received co-operation from all provincial governments and from the armed forces of Canada, which also have to make plans to cope with disasters which call for their assistance. They have such plans and are ready to implement them.
The initiative in seeking such assistance rests with the municipality which finds itself faced with a disaster with which it cannot deal. It then will call upon the province, and if the province finds it is faced with a disaster which is beyond its resources to cope with, it calls upon the federal government. Fortunately we are in the position to respond to such requests effectively and quickly.
The hon. gentleman also wondered how the Emergency Measures Organization was administered in the provinces. I think I gave a general indication of the role of this organization at the provincial level. Its role is to make plans to meet emergencies and to ensure that all agencies which would discharge these plans have in fact knowledge of the plans, have accepted them and made the necessary preparations. This is the role of the organization. It is not an executive agency but merely a planning and co-ordinating agency. That is the specific background.
Having regard to the representations of the hon. member for Saskatoon, I fully support the external aid programs of the government of Canada, although I am not responsible for their administration. In fact, they are quite irrelevant to the estimates we are discussing tonight. I wholeheartedly support the use, on a replacement basis, of our medical stockpile including the very efficient 200 bed dismantle-able and transportable hospitals, and I think the designers deserve a great deal of credit. I am pleased to note that the learned doctor shares that view.
As the hon. member pointed out, there have been shipments made of some ten of these hospitals to South Viet Nam, and more are to follow. I will refer his representation regarding doctors volunteering and serving in South Viet Nam to my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, under whose province perhaps this more particularly falls.

feel strongly that an endeavour to maintain at a high level interest in an organization whose functions in peacetime are relatively undramatic is doomed to failure, and that attempts to raise public interest in such an organization during peacetime will only result in a substantial let-down. It exists in name only. There are a number of foreign governments and agencies of foreign governments which are authorized to enter into contracts with other foreign corporations. They are not, however, authorized by their governments to enter into contracts with foreign governments.
This means for instance that the procurement service of the German army is under its statute allowed to enter into procurement contracts with foreign corporations, but if it should wish to enter into a contract with a foreign government it must proceed through the German foreign office, the Canadian foreign office and the Department of Defence Production. The process of procurement is vastly simplified if the German army procurement service is able to deal directly with the authorized entity in Canada and not have to proceed through the process on a formal government to government basis. This is the reason for the continued existence of the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
In practice what happens is that the foreign purchaser executes a contract with the Canadian Commercial Corporation. This is a contract between the crown corporation and the foreign purchaser. The same officials who have negotiated this contract immediately have the Department of Defence Production execute a contract in identical terms to the contract executed with the Canadian Commercial Corporation. They then proceed to act on that contract in terms of procurement, exactly as if it had been a contract entered into in the first place with the foreign government or agency.

How are we doing this? The minister has followed in the paths of the previous government which made incentives available back in 1960. That government allowed not only write-offs against tax, but a write-off of 50 per cent in respect of new work that was undertaken. This government thought that program was so good that they replaced it with the Industrial Research and Development Act, which does the same thing but also allows a cash grant of 25 per cent where research has been undertaken. We must admit that research in Canada has been very slow in developing. Perhaps the greatest research development in this country has been in the pulp and paper and chemical industries. I hope the minister will bear this fact in mind when considering tariffs in respect of the chemical industry, because this industry has done very well in Canada. The minister said he will have to protect some industries, and I hope this will be one of them.
The primary industries, in which we have for so long been engaged in Canada, require a minimum amount of research. A great deal of the raw materials and the semi-processed materials have been shipped out of this country to be processed in other countries and shipped back to us. The reason for this is obvious. We do not have the know-how to manufacture these articles and be competitive in so doing.
There is another factor to be considered in this respect. There are operating in Canada many subsidiary firms of American industries. I do not know whether people realize that most of the research in connection with these industries is carried out in the United States. The subsidiary firms operating in this

We have educated in this country many scientists who have crossed the border to the south. I was looking at the figures the other day and found that in 1964 over 4,000 professional and technical people crossed the border to the south. Many of them carried on research in the United States for the parent companies which have subsidiaries in Canada. Mr. Speaker, on May 31 I asked the government concerning recent representations made by the city of Vancouver requesting the Department of National Defence to permit the city of Vancouver the use of Jericho for park and recreational purposes. This is a very long standing request from the city of Vancouver, but it has been made again in very specific terms. I should like to make certain points which are very clearly and specifically made in this excellent brief from the city council. First of all, Jericho national defence lands break an almost continuous waterfront park system stretching from Stanley park to the north of the Fraser. Jericho national defence lands are one of the few consolidated areas still available to the city for the major park Vancouver needs in that area. In considering this, I must say that the provincial government has promised the release of its two waterlots which are adjacent to Jericho national defence lands if Ottawa will release Jericho. In other words,

When a man who has served ten years, always under the twilight of dishonour, should come before us with that sort of request, well, Mr. Speaker, my indignation does boil over, but not to the point that I cannot stop it at the moment to ask one question of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice. I would ask him this, whether there is a resignation under foot without any deals, with no promise of a pension being considered for L. A. Landreville of Sudbury, with no provisional pension promised, and with the government firmly bent on providing no pension under any circumstances?
If the Minister of Justice says yes to that at the moment, or no to that at the moment, then I will proceed accordingly. If he can assure me that no pension is promised to this miscreant judge under any circumstances I will sit down and he will hear no more from me. But if he cannot rise at this moment and say it is not promised under any circumstances, then I will not only pursue the matter now but I will pursue it on any other occasion I can; and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the government, that there will be many other members of this house, and not alone on this side, who will pursue it also.
Does the minister promise that? He sits silent.
In his career on the bench, which roughly, oddly enough, coincided with my career in parliament, Landreville did these things:
1.	He committed perjury before a parliamentary committee, before commissions and before various courts of Canada.
2.	He treated a commission of the highest court in the land, that is the committee of parliament, as a group of bumpkins who could be beguiled by loud protestations and long words.
3.	He was guilty of trying to put undue and unseemly pressure on the Liberal candidate in the Sudbury by-election to secure a pension.
4.	He was guilty of conduct unbecoming a judge when the R.C.M.P. came around to ask him what he was doing with regard to certain dealings with NONG stock.
5.	He was guilty of lack of candour and honesty in dealing with any authority and,

Now, there is a question here as to whether under the discretional provisions of the Judges Act any government should be allowed to give him a pension. I say, sir, that there is no question of discretion involved here at all, that he was guilty by any admission he might have made, by resignation before the guillotine fell on him in parliament.

speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member's time has expired.

maintopic: MR. JUSTICE LANDREVTLLE-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON POSSIBLE PAYMENT OF PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) asked me two questions. I am sorry I cannot read my own writing but I think I remember what the hon. member was saying. The first question was whether there was any deal, with provision to a pension, or something of that order. The answer is no. Neither the government nor myself made any deal with Mr. Justice Landreville regarding pension. The second question was whether the government was firmly bent on giving any such pension, and the answer is no. The government is not firmly bent on giving any pension.
Beyond those two simple answers, Mr. Speaker, if I have a moment I might comment on some other aspects of the hon. member's statement. He took offence at the fact that I said I would not give an undertaking to parliament that I would necessarily consult with it on this question, and I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) say "shame" when the answer was quoted as being no. There is nothing under the law of parliament or of the land that would make me give such an undertaking to parliament. Hon. members know the law pertaining to judges and to judges' pensions. They can read it.
There are cases where the government by order in council can give a pension. I have no intention of intimating that this is a case where the government would give a pension,
but the answer I gave was perfectly proper
because I stand by the letter of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: MR. JUSTICE LANDREVTLLE-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON POSSIBLE PAYMENT OF PENSION
speechtext:
As the hon. member knows,
Justice Landreville has been found guilty of no crime under the laws of this country. In the view of the parliamentary committee and of the commissioner, hon. Mr. Justice Hand, he has been found guilty of conduct, not on the bench but as a private person, guilty of conduct unbecoming a judge, that is to say, in meeting the high standards which we demand, and I think rightly so, of judges in this land. But he has been found guilty of no crime, and I personally do not subscribe to the kind of persecution upon which some members of the opposition seem to be bent since we got Justice Landreville's resignation.
Surely this is what we were hoping for. Surely hon. members were not looking forward with glee to the procedure of a joint parliamentary address. Surely if Mr. Justice Landreville resigned this should be the end of the matter, once the government has accepted the resignation. I do not share at all the kind of thinking which is behind the question asked by the hon. member of the opposition.
